text: Look closely at the wild curve from the last lesson, the one that threaded every noisy point. Its coefficients are enormous, some large and positive, others large and negative, cancelling each other almost perfectly at the data points and swinging apart everywhere in between. That suggests a remedy: keep the flexible model, but make large weights expensive, so the model only uses them when the data truly demands it.

The most common version is called L2 regularisation, or ridge. We add to the loss a penalty, lambda times the sum of the squared weights. Picture every weight tied to zero by a rubber band: the further it strays, the harder the band pulls back. In gradient descent this pull shows up as an extra term proportional to the weight itself, so at every step each weight shrinks by a small fraction before the data pushes it, which is why this is also called weight decay.

Lambda is a dial. At zero there is no penalty and we are back to the wild overfit curve. Turn it up and the curve calms down, bending only where the data insists. Turn it up too far and the bands win completely, flattening the weights so much that the model underfits. Somewhere in between sits the best setting, and we find it by checking error on held-out data.

A second penalty uses absolute values instead of squares: lambda times the sum of the sizes of the weights, called L1 regularisation, or the lasso. Its pull toward zero has the same strength no matter how small the weight already is, rather than fading as the weight shrinks. So small, unhelpful weights are pushed all the way to exactly zero, and the model quietly switches those features off, which makes L1 a tool for picking out the few features that matter.

The geometry shows why. Think of the penalty as a budget: the weights must stay inside a region around the origin. For L2 that region is a circle, for L1 it is a diamond with sharp corners on the axes. The loss forms oval contours around its unconstrained best point, and the solution is where the smallest oval first touches the region. A circle is usually touched at a smooth point where both weights are nonzero, while a diamond is very often touched at a corner, where one weight is exactly zero.

For linear regression, ridge even keeps a closed form. The normal equations gain one extra term, lambda times the identity matrix, added to X transpose X. That small addition has a second benefit: it makes the matrix safely invertible even when features are nearly copies of each other. One detail matters in practice: the intercept is usually left out of the penalty, because shifting the whole curve up or down is not the kind of complexity we want to punish.

Weight decay is part of how language models are trained today. The optimiser most commonly used for them, called Adam W, applies decay directly to the weights, separately from the gradient step, to keep them from growing without need. Next, we look at how to split data so that we can choose settings like lambda honestly.
